precedents.tender_scope: Mamul Yemek Alımı, Dağıtımı ve Sonrası Hizmetleri Alımı
precedents.daily_quantity_method: Previous week's corresponding days, with education term, break and summer periods treated in their own regimes
precedents.payment_basis: Monthly progress payment based on summed daily actual student/staff diners
precedents.excess_risk: Administration not responsible for excess; contractor cannot request payment for leftover produced meals
precedents.shortage_risk: Equivalent meal must be produced with Control Organization knowledge so service is not interrupted
product_implications: Contractor operations can be the direct daily quantity user while university remains buyer/control authority.
Historical-demand baseline is an actual contract-described operating heuristic.
Actual diners can provide both model ground truth and settlement reconciliation without PII if aggregated.
Excess and shortage have asymmetric operational/economic consequences.

precedents.daily_quantity_method: Previous meal counts, while accounting for academic calendar, menu and day popularity
precedents.payment_basis: Progress payment linked to actually eaten/purchased meal quantity
precedents.excess_risk: Administration not responsible for excess food; leftovers cannot simply be reused in another meal
precedents.shortage_risk: Insufficient preparation can trigger contractual penalty/service consequences
product_implications: Academic calendar and menu are contract-recognized demand drivers, not merely academic modeling ideas.
Decision loss should reflect excess cost and shortage/penalty risk rather than MAE alone.
Current heuristic baselines must include previous-demand and regime-aware approaches.

precedents.tender_scope: Sakarya Üniversitesi Servise Hazır Yemek Hizmeti Alım İşi
precedents.daily_quantity_method: Not promoted from this decision; the strong precedent is production-mix adjustment
precedents.menu_mix_rule: Default main-course mix includes 3% vegetarian and remaining selectable mains initially 50/50; contractor and university Control Organization may jointly increase the preferred selected main course using historical-period student/staff preference data
product_implications: Historical preference data can be contractually relevant to production mix even when total quantity is not the only decision.
Product architecture should separate total quantity, menu mix and campus allocation decisions.
A useful wedge may exist in mix optimization even if total meal quantity is constrained.
Dietary classes can be formal contract line items and should survive into the canonical data model.
Do not flatten contractually distinct service classes before decision modeling.

cross_precedent_patterns.claim: Daily production forecasting can be a contractor responsibility under university food-service contracts.
cross_precedent_patterns.product_effect: Treat contractor operations as a candidate daily user distinct from university buyer/control roles.

cross_precedent_patterns.claim: Excess and shortage can create asymmetric contract/operational risks.
cross_precedent_patterns.product_effect: Optimize decision loss/guardrails, not forecast MAE alone.

cross_precedent_patterns.claim: Actual diner/consumption quantity can be used for progress-payment settlement.
cross_precedent_patterns.product_effect: Where locally verified, aggregate actual-diner counts can reconcile model performance with contract settlement.

cross_precedent_patterns.claim: Academic calendar and menu context can be contract-recognized demand drivers.
cross_precedent_patterns.product_effect: Regime-aware and menu-aware historical baselines are mandatory benchmarks before complex models.

cross_precedent_patterns.claim: Reservation can be a permitted institutional mechanism for meal counts.
cross_precedent_patterns.product_effect: Keep reservation/pre-commit signals as a future option, not a forced current feature.

cross_precedent_patterns.claim: Historical preference data can alter production mix among menu alternatives.
cross_precedent_patterns.product_effect: Separate total-demand, menu-mix and campus-allocation decisions.

candidate_role_map.university_sks_food_services: contract owner, control authority, policy/menu/service governance
candidate_role_map.control_organization: service validation and possible joint operational decision authority
candidate_role_map.contractor_operations_kitchen: candidate direct daily quantity forecasting/production user
candidate_role_map.data_owner: card, turnstile, POS, reservation or transaction aggregate export
candidate_role_map.student_staff_diner: demand source and service beneficiary, not automatically buyer

candidate_commercial_hypothesis.label: HYPOTHESIS
candidate_commercial_hypothesis.statement: In some outsourced university dining contracts, operational value may be shared between university buyer/control functions and contractor production operations, making the problem closer to B2B2B decision support than a university-only sustainability dashboard.

cs1_requirements: Predict a demand distribution or decision range when asymmetry matters; do not rely only on point MAE.
Implement previous-same-weekday and regime-aware historical heuristics because these classes of rules appear in contract precedents.
Where verified, evaluate excess, shortage, emergency top-up, service failure and settlement-aware outcomes.
Do not express TL savings without local verified contract unit economics.
Separate total demand, menu mix and campus allocation heads only when corresponding operational decisions/data exist.
highest_value_bogazici_questions: Who forecasts quantity under the current TEMAŞ contract?
How is actual service counted for progress payment?
Can total quantity, campus allocation, menu mix or batch timing be changed independently?
forbidden_bogazici_inferences: Boğaziçi pays only for card-swiped meals.
TEMAŞ is contractually responsible for daily quantity forecasting at Boğaziçi.
Boğaziçi can change meal quantities daily.
Boğaziçi current contract uses reservation or smart-card settlement.
Contract precedents prove Boğaziçi savings or customer demand.
